text: A time series is a set of measurements taken in time order -- monthly sales, daily visits, hourly electricity use. Order matters: today depends on yesterday, so shuffled train-test splits need rethinking. Before forecasting anything, you need to see what the series is made of. Nearly every series is a combination of a few components.

Four components. Trend: the long-run direction, up, down, or flat. Seasonality: a pattern that repeats at a fixed, known period, like a December peak or a weekend dip. Cycles: rises and falls with no fixed length, easy to confuse with seasonality but calendar-free. Noise: what's left after removing the others -- ideally it looks random.

On five years of monthly sales we built ourselves, with a known trend of one point five units per month and a seasonal peak in November and December, seasonal_decompose with an additive model recovered a slope of one point five six against the true one point five, and a residual standard deviation of two point nine four against the true noise s.d. of four.

The recovered seasonal pattern had the right shape, with the big December peak, though individual months were off by a few units because noise leaks into the estimate. The trend had twelve missing values, because the classical method uses a centered moving average that can't be computed within six months of either end.

In an additive series, the seasonal swing has constant size: value equals trend plus seasonal plus noise. In a multiplicative series, the swing grows with the level: value equals trend times seasonal times noise. On a series built to scale that way, the yearly swing grew from about one hundred in year one to about one eighty-nine in year five, versus staying near seventy-five in the additive version.

Classical decomposition assumes the seasonal pattern never changes and leaves gaps at the ends. STL, Seasonal-Trend decomposition using Loess, allows the pattern to change slowly, can be made robust to outliers, and returns a value for every point -- on our series, stl.trend had no missing values at all.

Decomposition is a diagnostic, not a forecast -- it tells you whether a model needs a trend term, a seasonal term, or a log transform. Get the period right: twelve for monthly data with yearly seasonality, seven for daily data with weekly seasonality. Next, two properties that most classical forecasting models care about: stationarity and autocorrelation.
